sharedText: and never able to come to the knowledge of the
reason: A six-word run and the chapter's second-highest n-gram score, drawn purely by 'come to the knowledge of the' — 2 Timothy 3:7's silly women 'ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth', against Mosiah's 'that it might not come to the knowledge of the king'. The object is the whole sentence: Paul's is truth and Alma's is a hostile monarch, and 'come to the knowledge of' is a Book of Mormon formula that appears in the same chapter twice more (18:30, 18:31) with three different objects. Logged because the run is long enough to look like evidence and the same candidate returns at 18:31.

sharedText: in the day time from the
reason: Six words shared, and the sense is inverted at the preposition. Isaiah 4:6's tabernacle is 'for a shadow in the day time from the heat' — shelter from the sun, in a vision of Zion covered by cloud and fire; Mosiah 18:5's Alma 'did hide himself in the day-time, from the searches of the king' — concealment from a manhunt. What Isaiah's day-time refuge protects against is weather and what Alma's protects against is soldiers, and the two texts share the string only because both need to name a time of day and a thing to be sheltered from. Worth an entry because Isaiah 4:5-6's thicket-and-covering imagery is thematically close enough that a reader running on typology could accept it, and the 1830 hyphenation 'day-time' makes the match look more deliberate than it is.

Pure narrative connective; the five words carry no content and the two verses have nothing else in common. Passed over here rather than argued because the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 2:1 covers its kind, and recorded only because the score (2.00) put it at the head of the verse's candidate list. The real KJV background of Mosiah 18:11 — 'they clapped their hands for joy' — is the acclamation formula of 2 Kings 11:12 and Psalm 47:1, which the machine did not propose and which is too widely distributed to catalogue.

sharedText: that they should gather themselves together
reason: A six-word run at rarity 3.00, the highest score in the second half of the chapter, and it will not bear a link. 'Gather themselves together' stands in the KJV for armies, mourners, locusts and returning exiles alike; Ezra 10:7's proclamation summons the children of the captivity to Jerusalem to put away foreign wives, which has nothing to do with a weekly assembly for worship. The genuine background of Mosiah 18:25 is the sabbath-assembly language of Leviticus 23:3 ('an holy convocation') and the apostolic 'first day of the week' of Acts 20:7 and 1 Corinthians 16:2 — neither of which shares a phrase with the verse, which is why 18:25 gets no link at all despite being the chapter's most institutionally significant sentence.

Luke 20:20's spies watch Jesus so as to 'deliver him unto the power and authority of the governor', and the five-word run is real. It is superseded: the verse's borrowing is Acts 2:47's 'added to the church', a KJV singleton reproduced four words deep and carrying the whole clause, and 'the power and authority of God' is the Book of Mormon's own standing formula for priesthood rather than a borrowing from Luke's Roman jurisdiction. The link is at Acts 2:47. Recorded because the Lukan trial vocabulary is genuinely thick in these two chapters (Luke 23:2 at Mosiah 17:12, Luke 23:5 at Mosiah 18:33), which makes a third Lukan candidate here more tempting than it deserves — and that thickness is exactly the condition under which a false positive slips through.

Revelation 14:6's angel with the everlasting gospel 'to preach unto them that dwell on the earth' is a verse the Latter-day Saint tradition has strong reasons to look for, which is precisely why it should not be accepted on four words of connective tissue. The verse's real source is in the same clause and is not in doubt: 'the things pertaining to the kingdom of God' is an eight-word KJV singleton from Acts 1:3. The link is there.
